analysis.one_liner: Weakens Clean Air Act enforcement and gives tax breaks to small oil and gas wells.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, was sent to two House subcommittees and never received a hearing or vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rolled back major parts of the Clean Air Act: repealing EPA's power to require enhanced pollution monitoring, blocking any limit on chlorine compounds unless Congress specifically voted for one, making toxic air pollution standards weaker by requiring that compliance costs not exceed benefits, and letting companies keep the findings of their own environmental self-audits out of court. It also would have handed tax benefits to oil and gas producers, including a new credit of up to $3 per barrel for marginal wells and a lower federal gasoline tax of 15.3 cents instead of 18.4 cents per gallon. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been oil and gas producers, especially operators of low-producing "marginal" wells, who would get a new tax credit of $3 per barrel of oil and 50 cents per thousand cubic feet of gas, expanded percentage depletion for stripper wells, and faster write-offs for geological and geophysical exploration costs. Chemical makers, especially the chlorine industry, would gain because EPA could not restrict chlorine compounds without a new act of Congress. Refiners would gain from a lower 15.3-cent gasoline tax and the end of the minimum oxygen content requirement for reformulated gasoline. Companies of all kinds would gain from a privilege that keeps their voluntary environmental self-audits out of evidence in federal and state proceedings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers, chemical makers, refiners

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new tax credit of $3 per barrel of oil and 50 cents per thousand cubic feet of gas for production from marginal wells, and expands the definition of marginal production so more high-water stripper wells qualify for percentage depletion.
Lets oil and gas companies expense geological and geophysical exploration costs the same way they expense intangible drilling costs, reducing their current tax bills.

Prohibits EPA from banning or restricting the manufacture, use, or sale of chlorine compounds unless Congress specifically authorizes it after seeing a proposed rule, shielding the chlorine industry from future phase-outs.

Excludes waste used as a manufacturing feedstock from the legal definition of hazardous waste (with storage and distance limits), freeing factories that reuse their own waste streams from hazardous waste handling rules.

Makes voluntary environmental self-audit information privileged and inadmissible in federal or state proceedings, and bars penalties for violations disclosed through such audits, as long as the company promptly discloses and works toward compliance.
Reduces the federal gasoline excise tax to 15.3 cents per gallon for reformulated gasoline meeting a 2 percent oxygen content, and provides a 3-cent-per-gallon refund for gasoline used to make it.

Gives states more flexibility in running vehicle emissions inspection programs, allows moderate ozone areas two more years to meet air standards, and requires ozone readings to be averaged over 8 hours with an exceedance counted only above 0.10 ppm at two or more monitors, allowing up to four a year.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would absorb the cost of the new marginal well credits and the roughly 3-cent cut in the gasoline tax. People living near industrial facilities would bear the health side of weaker rules: no enhanced monitoring to verify compliance, air toxics standards capped at what companies can afford, self-audit information sealed from courts and agencies, longer deadlines for smoggy areas to clean up, and looser ozone counting that would let more violations go unrecorded. Communities relying on state air programs would also live with unapproved state permit programs in the meantime.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people breathing industrial-area air

drawbacks.text: Repealing EPA's enhanced monitoring authority and compliance certification requirements would remove the main federal tool for verifying that major polluters actually meet their permit limits, leaving violations harder to detect.

Capping every hazardous air pollutant standard at the level where compliance costs do not exceed benefits, and forcing a rewrite of standards issued since 1990, would weaken protection from toxic air emissions near industrial plants.

Making self-audit reports privileged and inadmissible could keep evidence of pollution out of court even in lawsuits brought by injured neighbors, and the carve-out only covers intentional violations and knowing endangerment, not ordinary negligence cases.
The chlorine provision would require a new act of Congress before EPA could restrict any chlorine compound, indefinitely delaying action on chemicals of public-health concern.

The marginal well credit and lower gasoline tax would reduce federal revenue; the credit is set at $3 per barrel and only phases out once oil prices rise from $17 to $25, meaning it pays out most when prices are already low for producers.

Extending moderate ozone attainment deadlines from 6 to 8 years, and letting regions record at most four 8-hour ozone exceedances a year at two monitors, would leave residents of smoggy areas breathing unhealthy air longer and make air quality data look better than it is.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a few genuine conveniences: more state flexibility in vehicle testing, a slightly lower gas tax, and help for small stripper-well operators in a low-price era. But the core of the bill is a broad rollback of Clean Air Act enforcement and toxics standards, a legal shield for chlorine, and a secrecy privilege for companies' self-audits, all paid for by taxpayers and by people living near polluting facilities. The costs plainly outweigh the benefits, which is one reason not a single member of either party signed on.

outcome.mechanism: A single lawmaker's bill was referred to two House subcommittees in May 1996, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and quietly died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stockman introduced the bill in the House on May 10, 1996, with no cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, on the day it was introduced.
On May 23, 1996, it was sent to two Energy and Commerce subcommittees, Health and Environment, and Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's action history ends at the subcommittee referral, and the Congress expired on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public kept the existing Clean Air Act safeguards, monitoring requirements, and chlorine oversight the bill would have weakened, and taxpayers were spared the cost of the oil and gas credits. No industry got anything; the only winners from the outcome were ordinary people breathing the air.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, by keeping existing safeguards

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to analyze: the bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it attracted zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill hands them a new $3-per-barrel credit for marginal wells, expanded depletion for high-water stripper wells, and faster expensing of exploration costs, all paid for by taxpayers. Some relief for small operators in oil busts is a real interest, but it comes bundled with weaker air pollution rules.

The bill bars EPA from restricting any chlorine compound without a new act of Congress, and exempts manufacturing feedstock from hazardous waste rules, cutting compliance costs while leaving the public to rely on slower, more political chemical oversight.

A lower 15.3-cent gasoline tax, a 3-cent refund on feedstock gasoline, and repeal of the minimum oxygen content mandate all cut refiners' costs. Drivers share some of the gas tax benefit, which is why the stance is mixed.
Repeal of enhanced monitoring, cost-capped air toxics standards, and a court-proof privilege for self-audits would make violations cheaper and harder to prove for facilities of every kind.

Repealing the minimum oxygen content requirement for reformulated gasoline removes a guaranteed market for oxygenates like ethanol. Drivers benefit from flexibility; the ethanol industry loses a mandate-driven customer base.

Excluding manufacturing feedstock from the hazardous waste definition shrinks the stream of material that must be handled and billed as hazardous. Factories save money; the disposal industry loses business, and the public relies on the bill's 90-day and 25-mile limits for safety.
